hero.title: Entooma Sidai: A Maasai Mara Rangeland Restoration and Conservation Project
hero.subtitle: Climate Investment Partners, in partnership with Entooma Sidai Limited, has committed 500,000 hectares of degraded grasslands in Narok County, Kenya to restoration through sustainable grazing management — protecting one of the world's most iconic wildlife ecosystems.

ind.area-managed.why: Restoring grassland at this scale changes what the land can do. Healthier grass holds soil in place, lets rain soak in instead of running off, and leaves more forage for both livestock and wildlife through the dry season.
ind.land-cover-baseline.title: Land cover in Narok County (regional context)
ind.land-cover-baseline.definition: Distribution of land cover types across Narok County — the region surrounding the project, not a survey of the project's own boundary.
ind.land-cover-baseline.why: Overgrazing has degraded grasslands across the wider region, reducing grass biodiversity, inhibiting regeneration, and decreasing forage for both livestock and wildlife. This regional picture is the backdrop the project's own restoration work sits against.
ind.land-cover-baseline.caveats: These figures describe land cover across Narok County as a whole (Feasibility Study, Table 1, p.21), not the project's own boundary. Three different area figures appear across the project's documents — the project description's initial, pre-delimitation area (about 883,500 ha), the GIS-measured boundary on file (about 652,000 ha), and CIP's confirmed final project area (500,000 ha) — and none of them is what this chart measures. Shown here as regional context only, not as the project's own baseline.
ind.wildlife-corridor.why: Animals moving between the two parks cross land that people also graze. How that land is managed is what decides whether the route stays open.
ind.key-species.title: Key species by conservation status
ind.key-species.definition: The species whose habitat corridors the project is intended to restore, each listed with its status on the IUCN Red List.
ind.key-species.why: Through the implementation of community driven sustainable grazing management practices, the project will restore valuable wildlife habitat corridors for a range of species.
ind.key-species.caveats: Named in the project's public design document, which identifies the black rhino specifically. Project materials also list the African savanna elephant, giraffe and cheetah as IUCN Red List species in the area. This demo leads with the black rhino because it carries the highest conservation status.
ind.communities-engaged.why: Rotational grazing only works if neighbours move their herds together. The governance structure is what makes that agreement hold, which is why it is reported here instead of a headcount.
ind.womens-participation.title: Women's participation as a design objective
ind.womens-participation.definition: How the project is set up to include women in the work it creates and in the decisions about how its benefits are shared.
ind.womens-participation.why: Employment in remote rangeland is seasonal and unevenly available to women. Writing gender-equitable income into the project design — rather than reporting on it afterwards — is what makes participation something the project can be held to.
ind.womens-participation.caveats: This is a stated design commitment, not a measured outcome. No participation figure exists in any of the project's documents, so none is shown here.
ind.local-jobs.why: Conservation work that pays local wages gives people a reason to keep it going once the funding cycle ends.
ind.benefit-sharing.why: Tying household income to the condition of the rangeland is what lines conservation up with the way people already use the land.

stories.title: Stories from the project area
story.rangeland.title: What overgrazing took, and what rest gives back
story.rangeland.alt: Open grassland stretching to low hills under a wide sky, dotted with scattered trees and shrubs.
story.rangeland.body: Grazing the same ground without pause thinned the grass here, emptied the seed bank and let invasive plants move in. Less grass meant less forage, for cattle and for wildlife alike. Moving herds on a planned rotation gives the ground time between grazings: grass recovers, roots hold the soil, and rain soaks in instead of running off.
story.migration.title: The crossing runs through working land
story.migration.alt: A herd of wildebeest fording a shallow river between wooded banks during the annual migration.
story.migration.body: The route between the Maasai Mara National Reserve and the Serengeti does not stop at a park boundary. Part of it runs across land that families graze and farm every day. Whether the corridor stays open is decided less by the parks than by how that in-between land is managed.
story.herder.title: The rotation only works if neighbours agree
story.herder.alt: A herder walking behind cattle at dusk, silhouetted against an orange sky with a lone acacia tree.
story.herder.body: One family resting its pasture achieves very little if the neighbouring herd grazes it the next morning. So the plan is built around groups: herders who agree to move their animals together, grazing officers they elect themselves, and a committee that keeps the wider schedule honest. The governance is the intervention.

about.title: How to read this brief
about.intro: This brief reports what the project’s own documents say, and marks plainly where they say nothing. That makes it read differently from a standard investment summary in a few specific ways, and they are worth knowing before you judge the substance. Four conventions cover almost everything on the page.
about.states.title: Four ways a figure can appear
about.states.body: A figure is either sourced, absent, disputed, or part of a section nobody has provided yet, and each looks different on purpose. A sourced figure carries a small green square and a citation naming the document, sheet or page it came from. An absent figure says “Not stated in source” at the same size a real figure would have taken, with the reason underneath — it is never greyed out or left blank. A disputed figure shows both numbers in crimson, because two documents genuinely disagree and resolving that is not this brief’s call to make. A section nobody has provided yet shows a hatched panel rather than quietly disappearing. The vocabulary is the same in every section, so it only has to be learned once.
about.sources.title: What a source line promises — and what it does not
about.sources.body: Every figure here is traceable to a named document and a date, down to the workbook cell or page where it appears. That is what the source line guarantees. It does not guarantee the figure is right. Nothing in this brief has been through third-party validation — the project is at feasibility stage, not validated — so “sourced” means “we can show you where this came from”, not “someone independent has checked it”. Where a figure carries a qualifier that changes how it should be read, that qualifier appears beneath it as a caveat rather than in a footnote.
about.figures.title: How the numbers are shown
about.figures.body: Figures are reported exactly as their source states them: never recalculated, never reconciled against another document, never rounded to make a case look tidier. Where a source states a date as a year, it renders as a year rather than being padded to a month or a day. Large amounts and long decimals are shortened for reading — 50B rather than fifty thousand million, 1.51 rather than sixteen decimal places — but the exact value always appears immediately beneath, beside the citation. Nothing on this page is a figure we produced.
about.flag.title: The black-and-yellow flag
about.flag.body: One item on the page is marked in hazard colours, and it is meant to look out of place. It marks something known to be wrong and already assigned for correction — in this version, the mapped boundary, which is drawn from a shapefile predating the confirmation of the final project area. It is deliberately not styled like the rest of the brief, because anything that looks designed also looks finished, and this is neither. When the corrected file arrives, the flag is deleted rather than restyled.
about.credits.title: How this is maintained, and by whom
about.credits.body: There is no content management system and no database. Every figure, caveat and citation lives in a small set of JSON files that are checked on every change against a schema and a validator — a figure cannot be added without a source, and a section cannot be marked absent without a stated reason. Built by Daniel Collante and Marcel Rodríguez. Project developer: Climate Investment Partners. Map basemap by Stadia Maps with an automatic OpenStreetMap fallback.
